\section[cūriōsus, cūriōsa, cūriōsum]{cūriōsus, cūriōsa, cūriōsum — inquisitive, painstaking}

\label{lesson:LA-C212-curiosus}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for in vain, then the Latin for back again.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: cūriōsus, cūriōsa, cūriōsum}
\textbf{cūriōsus, cūriōsa, cūriōsum} — \textquotedblleft{}inquisitive, painstaking\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{cūriōsus} is built on \emph{cūra}, \textquotedblleft{}care\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), with \emph{-ōsus}, \textquotedblleft{}full of\textquotedblright{}: full of care, so careful or prying. English \emph{curious} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{cūriōsus, cūriōsa, cūriōsum}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{cūriōsus, cūriōsa, cūriōsum}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{cūriōsus, cūriōsa, cūriōsum}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for in vain, then the Latin for back again, then say \emph{cūriōsus, cūriōsa, cūriōsum} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does cūriōsus, cūriōsa, cūriōsum mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Inquisitive, painstaking\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[invidus, invida, invidum]{invidus, invida, invidum — envious}

\label{lesson:LA-C212-invidus}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for back again, then the Latin for inquisitive.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: invidus, invida, invidum}
\textbf{invidus, invida, invidum} — \textquotedblleft{}envious\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{invidus} is built on \emph{invideō}, \textquotedblleft{}to look askance at, to envy\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), from \emph{in}, \textquotedblleft{}against\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{videō}, \textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{}. English \emph{envy} comes from the same family.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{invidus, invida, invidum}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for back again, then the Latin for inquisitive, then say \emph{invidus, invida, invidum} again
\end{itemize}

\textbf{anxius, anxia, anxium} — \textquotedblleft{}anxious\textquotedblright{}.

\section[tacitus, tacita, tacitum]{tacitus, tacita, tacitum — silent}

\label{lesson:LA-C212-tacitus}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for anxious, then the Latin for peaceful.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: tacitus, tacita, tacitum}
\textbf{tacitus, tacita, tacitum} — \textquotedblleft{}silent\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{tacitus} is the past participle of \emph{taceō}, \textquotedblleft{}to be silent\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short): passed over in silence, then silent. English \emph{tacit} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

One more word for this chapter.

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for anxious, then the Latin for peaceful, then say \emph{tacitus, tacita, tacitum} again
\end{itemize}
